title: Protein: g/lb vs g/kg — Fitness Targets Reconciled
h1: Protein intake — g/lb vs g/kg, what the studies actually show
description: 0.8 g/lb ≈ 1.76 g/kg. The '1 g per pound of bodyweight' rule doubles the RDA. Full evidence-based targets by goal, and the diminishing-return point.

hero: The gym rule of thumb '1 gram per pound' converts to 2.2 g/kg — nearly triple the RDA of 0.8 g/kg. Actual protein optima for muscle hypertrophy sit at 1.6–2.2 g/kg (0.73–1.0 g/lb) by meta-analysis; anything above ~2.4 g/kg gives no additional muscle synthesis.
body: Protein-per-bodyweight targets are the single most cited fitness metric, and they exist in two systems that don't agree at a glance. US strength training literature quotes g/lb; sports nutrition papers use g/kg; the RDA uses g/kg. Cross-referencing without conversion produces recommendations off by a factor of 2.
## The exact factors

> 1 g/lb = 2.2046 g/kg
> 1 g/kg = 0.4536 g/lb
> RDA (US/UK): 0.8 g/kg = 0.36 g/lb (adult minimum)
> ISSN hypertrophy: 1.4–2.0 g/kg = 0.64–0.91 g/lb
> Cutting/deficit target: 2.2–2.6 g/kg = 1.0–1.2 g/lb
> Practical ceiling: 2.4 g/kg (Morton 2018 meta-analysis)
## Targets by goal, both units

| Goal | g/kg | g/lb | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| RDA (minimum, sedentary) | 0.8 | 0.36 | US/EU official |
| General health, active | 1.0-1.2 | 0.45-0.55 | ACSM 2019 |
| Endurance training | 1.2-1.6 | 0.55-0.73 | ISSN 2017 |
| Hypertrophy (bulking) | 1.6-2.2 | 0.73-1.0 | Morton 2018 meta |
| Cutting (deficit) | 2.2-2.6 | 1.0-1.2 | Helms 2014 |
| Elderly (sarcopenia prevention) | 1.2-1.6 | 0.55-0.73 | PROT-AGE 2013 |
| Practical ceiling | 2.4 | 1.09 | Morton 2018 |
## Worked example — 80 kg (176 lb) lifter
**RDA:** 80 × 0.8 = 64 g. About 2 chicken breasts. Enough to prevent muscle loss; not enough to build.
**Hypertrophy target (mid):** 80 × 1.9 = 152 g. About 5 palm-sized protein portions across the day.
**Cutting target:** 80 × 2.3 = 184 g. Requires deliberate high-protein meals plus a whey shake.
**'1 g/lb' bro rule:** 176 g — falls inside the cutting range, above the maintenance/hypertrophy optimum.
## Where the '1 g/lb' rule came from

1980s bodybuilding — an easy mental target. The number sits above the physiological optimum (~0.8 g/lb) but below the ceiling (~1.1 g/lb). It survives because it works: high enough for muscle protein synthesis to be saturated, low enough to fit a mixed diet. Not because it is precisely calibrated.
## The Morton 2018 ceiling

The definitive meta-analysis (49 studies, 1863 participants, Br J Sports Med) found lean-mass gains plateau at 1.62 g/kg (95% CI: 1.03–2.20). The 95% CI upper is 2.20 g/kg — beyond this, extra protein displaces training-adaptation nutrients and provides no additional benefit. This has been replicated in Antonio (2015) and Bandegan (2017).
## Per-meal distribution matters

Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) saturates at ~0.4 g/kg per meal (~30–45 g for most adults, higher for larger athletes). Eating 200 g at dinner is not equivalent to 4 × 50 g meals — the single-meal ceiling wastes ~40 g into gluconeogenesis. Aim for 3–5 protein-anchored meals per day.
## Leucine threshold

The specific trigger for MPS is leucine content, ~2.5–3 g per meal. Whey has ~11% leucine (25 g whey = 2.75 g leucine — exactly at the threshold). Plant sources have lower leucine density: pea protein 8%, rice protein 7%. Vegan lifters typically aim 20–25% higher total protein to compensate.
## Kidney load and 'high protein is dangerous'

The old claim — high protein damages kidneys — has been repeatedly falsified in healthy people (Devries 2018 meta-analysis). It is a real concern for pre-existing renal disease; otherwise, 2.2 g/kg has not been shown to affect kidney function even long-term. The confusion comes from creatinine rising with muscle mass (a lab marker, not damage).
## Timing — the anabolic window myth

Post-workout protein within 30 minutes was a 2000s belief. Evidence (Schoenfeld 2013 meta): total daily protein matters far more than timing. Protein within 3 hours of training is fine; the anabolic window is closer to a garage door than a keyhole.
## Practical protein sources by weight

| Food | Protein per 100 g | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Chicken breast (cooked) | 31 g | Complete AA |
| Beef sirloin (cooked) | 29 g | Complete AA |
| Salmon (cooked) | 25 g | Complete AA + omega-3 |
| Tuna (canned in water) | 26 g | Complete AA |
| Greek yogurt (0% fat) | 10 g | Cheap, complete |
| Eggs | 13 g | Complete AA gold standard |
| Tofu (firm) | 15 g | Complete AA |
| Lentils (cooked) | 9 g | Incomplete — pair with grain |
| Whey protein powder | 75-80 g | 25 g per scoop |
| Casein powder | 78 g | Slow-release |
## The five-second recap

Multiply bodyweight in kg by 1.6–2.2 for hypertrophy; 2.2–2.6 for cutting. In pounds, that is roughly 0.75–1.0 for building, 1.0–1.2 for cutting. Above 2.4 g/kg gives no additional muscle. Split across 3–5 meals with 25–45 g each.

faqs.q: Is 1 g per pound too much?
faqs.a: It is above the optimum but under the ceiling. About 2.2 g/kg — well-tolerated in healthy adults, but no more muscle than 1.8 g/kg would give. Fine as an easy mental target.

faqs.q: Do I count protein from bread and rice?
faqs.a: Yes — all sources count toward the daily total. Bread ~8 g protein per slice; rice ~4 g per 100 g cooked. These are 'complete' only when combined with legumes; individually they are protein-restricted.

faqs.q: Does high protein cause bone loss?
faqs.a: No — a 2000s hypothesis that has not survived controlled trials. High-protein diets do not leach calcium from bones in healthy adults. In fact, higher protein is associated with better BMD in the elderly.

faqs.q: How much protein for weight loss?
faqs.a: 2.2–2.6 g/kg while in a caloric deficit — preserves lean mass and increases satiety. The extra thermic effect (protein has ~25% TEF vs 5% for carbs/fat) also raises daily energy expenditure ~50–100 kcal.

faqs.q: Is whey better than plant protein?
faqs.a: Whey has higher leucine density and faster absorption — best for muscle response per gram. Plant proteins are equivalent when total daily intake is 20–25% higher to match leucine. For most people, the source matters less than the total.
